source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Only paper found that ties fast-and-frugal theory directly to LLM behaviour. Theory: an agent unsure of its own cue precision should stop after k high-validity cues (matches take-the-best under a Descending Dominance condition). Prediction: longer chain of thought hurts on items with high meta-uncertainty. Pre-registered test supported it.
numbers: 7 models (phi3.5 3.8B, mistral 7B, Qwen2.5 7B/14B/32B, claude-sonnet-4-5, gpt-4o), 5 CoT-length conditions, 7,875 responses, FEH-79 Knightian items vs matched controls. Interaction negative at posterior 1.00; pooled high-regime accuracy drop 17.3 points (95% CrI 7.7 to 25.5); controls with definite answers show no cost.
quote: a Bayesian agent whose own precision is uncertain has a rational incentive to truncate cue integration after a small number of high-validity cues
limits: Single-author preprint, not peer reviewed. Regime assigned by item category, not by the continuous score. Scoring was machine-checked recognition of indeterminacy; 46 expert-panel items deferred. No reasoning-trained models (o1, R1 style) tested.
agent_relevance: Supports an S0 rule: on items with no base rate or verifier, cap reasoning at a few steps and prefer abstaining or committing early. Matches G1, G11, G12.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics, per-model results
finding: The less-is-more effect in CoT is not universal. It is strong in mid-size open models, weak or inconclusive in frontier models, reversed in the smallest model.
numbers: Interaction (log-odds, negative = degradation): Qwen2.5 32B -2.92 [-4.05,-1.81]; Qwen2.5 7B -2.86 [-3.81,-1.94]; Qwen2.5 14B -2.23 [-3.29,-1.17]; gpt-4o -0.89 [-2.15,+0.39]; claude-sonnet-4-5 -0.80 [-2.08,+0.48] (Pr<0 = 0.884); phi3.5 reversed (+0.98). Direct prompt gave the correct 'cannot be determined' about three-quarters of the time; step-by-step cut it, by nearly 40 points in qwen2.5:14b.
limits: Frontier models only directional. Realized-step-count analysis reverses sign (endogenous), so only assigned length is causal.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the heuristic gate helps equally on every backbone; the S0 gate should be measured on our own model.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 text-davinci-002 shows heuristics-and-biases errors on standard vignettes but fails in non-human ways when vignettes are changed. Closest early test of the judgment paradigms.
numbers: 12 of 12 standard vignettes answered correctly or with a human-like mistake. Fell for conjunction fallacy (Linda) and the hospital problem (judged about equal); did NOT show base-rate neglect on the cab problem. All 3 CRT items answered with the intuitive wrong answer. Adversarial rewordings (for example 'Wrong CRT', 'Reverse Wason') gave mistakes that were neither correct nor human-like.
quote: GPT-3, just like people, fell for the same congruence bias
limits: One model (GPT-3). Vignettes may be in training data. No take-the-best, recognition or cue-based tasks were run.
agent_relevance: Surface resemblance to human heuristics is not evidence the model uses a heuristic; test with altered items.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT (preprint title: Thinking fast and slow in LLMs)
finding: Intuitive (System-1-like) errors on the CRT and semantic illusions rise with GPT-3 scale and then vanish in ChatGPT, which uses chain of thought by default.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks. Humans: 38% correct (41% in original, n=3,428). GPT-3-davinci-003: 5% correct, 80% intuitive-wrong. ChatGPT-3.5: 59% correct, 15% intuitive. ChatGPT-4: 96% correct, 0% intuitive. Chain of thought in 97% (3.5) and 84-85% (4) of responses. Suppressing CoT ('shortest possible answer'): ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged (diff 4%, p=.49); ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%. CoT instruction on davinci-003: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%.
limits: CRT items are public and may be memorized; authors add new generated variants. Math ability is a confound, partly handled by semantic illusions.
agent_relevance: Newer models carry trained intuition that survives forced short answers on known trap classes: a direct mode is safe only where the class is well covered. Informs S0 mode choice.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR)
finding: Large meta-analysis plus own tests: CoT gains are concentrated on math and symbolic tasks; elsewhere direct answering is about as good. Nearest empirical support for a gate that skips deliberation.
numbers: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus 20 datasets x 14 models. Average CoT gain: math 14.2, symbolic 12.3, logical 6.9 points (category averages as reported). On MMLU and MMLU Pro, about 95% of the CoT gain is on questions containing '='.
quote: As much as 95% of the total performance gain from CoT on MMLU is attributed to questions containing
limits: Mostly pre-reasoning-model era. Gain size depends on prompt and model.
agent_relevance: S0 can route non-symbolic, non-verifiable classes to direct mode and save compute with little loss.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): CoT can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (ICML)
finding: Uses the human 'verbal thinking hurts' literature as a heuristic to find LLM tasks where CoT hurts. It worked on 3 of 6 tasks.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar): GPT-4o 87.5% to 64.4% with CoT (-23.1, p<.0001); o1-preview subset 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0% (36.3-point gap); Claude 3.5 Sonnet unchanged (65.9 to 67.7). Face recognition: all 6 LMMs worse, e.g. GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2, Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6. Exceptions task: GPT-4o needs 12.5 rounds with CoT vs 2.9 direct (+331%). Bootstrap against 378 comparisons from Sprague: none of 100,000 resamples showed a larger mean drop.
limits: Three other tasks (spatial intuition, NLI, aggregating features across 4 apartments) showed mixed or positive CoT effects, because models differ from humans (long context, no motor simulation).
agent_relevance: Concrete task types for S0 to label think-less: pattern recognition without articulable rules, perceptual matching, learning rules with exceptions.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute (TMLR)
finding: Longer reasoning lowers accuracy on distractor counting, spurious-feature regression and constraint tracking; failure patterns differ by model family. Closest large-model analogue of more cues, less accuracy.
numbers: Tasks: Misleading Math/Python (500 questions per distractor count n=1..5), Grades Regression (500 students, 0/8/16-shot), Zebra puzzles. Regression zero-shot: Claude Sonnet 3.7, Claude Opus 4 and o3-mini show inverse scaling in the controlled setup; Sonnet 4, o4-mini, o3 flat or noisy; Qwen3-32B positive. Few-shot examples largely corrected the spurious-feature reliance.
limits: Controlled budgets via prompt keywords; effect varies by model and setup. Some settings show positive scaling.
agent_relevance: Regression with spurious features is an LLM version of the cue-selection problem take-the-best addresses: few-shot grounding beat extra thinking.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Builds 13,465 prompts testing prompt-induced (anchoring, framing, status quo, group attribution), sequential and inherent (primacy) biases in LLM admissions-style decisions, and tests mitigation by awareness, contrastive, counterfactual, few-shot and self-help prompts.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; mitigation arms: self-awareness, contrastive, counterfactual, few-shot, self-help (model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias). Authors report self-help debiasing works without hand-crafted examples. Per-model gains not extracted.
limits: I did not extract per-model percentages; two-column text was hard to parse. Not a fast-and-frugal test.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level debiasing is cheap but must be measured per bias; background for S1 input hygiene.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks (PNAS Nexus)
finding: Models, like humans, reason better when semantic content supports the logical answer; belief and content bias is shared. Pretrained priors enter reasoning like an ecological prior.
numbers: Three tasks: NLI, syllogisms, Wason selection. Models include Chinchilla, PaLM 2 family, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5; same direction of content effects as humans, bootstrapped CIs in figures (exact accuracies not extracted).
limits: Effect sizes by model not extracted this session.
agent_relevance: A model's world knowledge is a cue source; content shortcuts are expected and need conflict items to detect.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases (NeurIPS)
finding: Uses cognitive biases to predict Codex failures: framing, anchoring (outputs move toward an anchor function in the prompt) and frequency bias (copying common training patterns).
numbers: Case study on Codex code generation; qualitative result that errors are predictable from human bias analogues (counts not extracted).
limits: One code model; older.
agent_relevance: Anchors in context bias generation: supports fresh context per attempt at S3.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld & Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned LMs exhibit emergent cognitive bias (TACL)
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief biases. Bias is stronger in instruction-tuned models than in base counterparts.
numbers: Biases: decoy effect, certainty effect, belief bias. Models: GPT-3, Mistral, T5 families incl. Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Per-model effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Per-model effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Alignment tuning may install human-like shortcuts; do not treat the aligned model as a neutral reasoner.

source: Opedal et al. (2024) Do language models exhibit the same cognitive biases in problem solving as human learners? (ICML)
finding: Tests children's math-word-problem biases in LLMs across comprehension, planning and execution. Some biases mirror those in children, others do not.
numbers: Neuro-symbolic generation of word problems with controlled features; LLMs show some child-like biases (number-frequency effect noted). Per-bias numbers not extracted.
limits: Per-bias numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Item-feature-controlled test sets are the method to copy for our own S0 class studies.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do not think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend far more tokens than needed on trivial problems; most extra solutions add nothing. Self-training toward shorter solutions cut tokens without hurting accuracy.
numbers: On '2 plus 3' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. Test sets ASDIV < GSM8K < MATH500 in difficulty. QwQ-32B-Preview and R1 tested.
limits: Efficiency study, not a heuristics test; overthinking is measured waste, not always an accuracy loss.
agent_relevance: Supports G12 spend-by-difficulty: a cheap difficulty gate at S0.

source: Zhang, Lin, Hou, Feng & Li (2025) AdaptThink: reasoning models can learn when to think
finding: A trained gate that picks Thinking or NoThinking by difficulty beats always-thinking. NoThinking is equal or better on simple problems.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: response length cut 50.9% (GSM8K), 63.5% (MATH500), 44.7% (AIME2024) with accuracy +4.1, +1.4, +1.6 points respectively. Averaged over math sets: length -53%, accuracy +2.4%.
limits: Needs RL training, which our approach avoids; small distilled models.
agent_relevance: Direct empirical case for the S0 gate; our version must be a prompt-level or scaffold classifier.

source: Chen, Zaharia & Zou (2023) FrugalGPT: how to use LLMs while reducing cost and improving performance
finding: LLM cascade: ask cheap models first and stop at the first answer that passes a learned reliability score. Structurally a fast-and-frugal stopping rule over models instead of cues.
numbers: Matches best single LLM (GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction, or +4% accuracy at same cost.
limits: Needs a trained scorer per task. Cost, not psychology, motivated it.
agent_relevance: A cascade with a check at each stage is an S0/S4 pattern: stop on the first passing check (G1).

source: Ong et al. (2025) RouteLLM: learning to route LLMs with preference data (ICLR)
finding: Router sends easy queries to a weak model and hard ones to a strong model; keeps most of the quality at much lower cost.
numbers: Reports MT Bench score at 50% strong-model calls equal to 95% of GPT-4's (8.8); GSM8K at 95% of GPT-4 quality with reduced calls. Other ratios not extracted.
limits: Trained routers using preference data.
agent_relevance: A class-level gate at S0 is the same decision as routing.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam & Kambhampati (2025) Chain of thoughtlessness? An analysis of CoT in planning (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: CoT gains in Blocksworld exist only when prompts are very specific to the problem class, and fade as problem size grows past the examples.
numbers: Two LLMs, Blocksworld stacks; improvements collapse as stack size n exceeds example size (exact accuracies not extracted).
limits: Planning only; older models.
agent_relevance: Reasoning scaffolds do not generalize past their example distribution: check class coverage at S0.

source: Hug (2023) How do referees integrate evaluation criteria into their overall judgment? Evidence from grant peer review
finding: Recent human test of fast-and-frugal trees against logistic regression on real expert judgment. Regression slightly better; trees close.
numbers: Career-funding dataset, 2 referees per application, training set n=237. Logistic regression predicted overall assessment slightly better than FFTs. Also restates Czerlinski et al. (1999): take-the-best 71% vs multiple regression 68% over 20 environments, using 2.4 vs 7.7 cues on average.
limits: Czerlinski figures are second-hand through this paper. Author concludes referees use many criteria and complex rules, undercutting the uniform frugal style.
agent_relevance: Boundary case: with enough data and many informative cues, compensatory models match or beat frugal trees.

source: Chen, Fu, Krishna & Menzies (2018) Applications of psychological science for actionable analytics (FSE)
finding: Fast-and-frugal trees for software defect prediction: tiny trees (5 lines or fewer) beat standard learners in many cases.
numbers: FFT statistically better in 43 of 56 comparisons (77%) in the reported matrix; better on dist2heaven and Popt; strong when training is restricted to operational attributes.
limits: Software datasets; metric choice favours recall/false-alarm balance.
agent_relevance: Older AI system built on FFTs; shows frugal trees are a viable readable checker for triage.

source: Agrawal, Tu & Menzies (2018) Can you explain that, better? Comprehensible text analytics for SE applications
finding: LDA features plus fast-and-frugal trees classify NASA bug reports with small human-readable rules and similar or better performance than complex text miners.
numbers: Six NASA bug-report datasets; FFT on LDA topics reported as matching or beating complex methods (exact scores not extracted).
limits: Older SE data; reported by authors.
agent_relevance: Short readable decision rules over a few derived features could serve as S0 class tables.

source: Peltola, Jokinen & Kaski (2019) Probabilistic formulation of the Take The Best heuristic (CogSci)
finding: Reformulates take-the-best as a likelihood model so cue order and direction are learned from data by Bayesian inference, with no tunable parameters under uniform priors.
numbers: Model paper; compares to ABC-TTB and standard TTB on benchmark data (numbers not extracted).
limits: Small benchmark sets.
agent_relevance: Learning cue order from our own S0 outcome logs is feasible and cheap.

source: Schulz, Speekenbrink & Meder (2016) Simple trees in complex forests: growing Take The Best by approximate Bayesian computation
finding: ABC-TTB learns cue order and direction from building blocks and can outperform traditional TTB while trading off effort and performance explicitly.
numbers: Proof-of-concept simulations; recovers data generated by TTB.
limits: Proof of concept only.
agent_relevance: Shows the heuristic can be learned online rather than fixed by hand.

source: Jagadish, Thalmann, Coda-Forno, Binz & Schulz (2026) Meta-learning ecological priors from LLMs explains human learning and decision making (ERMI)
finding: LLMs generate ecologically valid tasks; a meta-learned model trained on them reproduces which heuristic people use in paired comparison: one-reason when cue ranks are known, equal weighting when directions are known.
numbers: Paired comparison: Gini over weights M=0.3399 (SEM 0.0631) in ranking condition (one-reason), 0.0743 (SEM 0.0138) in direction condition (equal weights), 0.1794 (SEM 0.0333) in unknown condition (weighted). ERMI best fit to human choices in 2-attribute (M PMF 0.7299, SEM 0.0888) and 4-attribute (0.6284, SEM 0.0897) experiments. 15 experiments overall.
quote: ERMI uses the same heuristics that people use in the respective condition
limits: Model fit to human data, not an LLM agent test. Needs LLM task generation to match real statistics.
agent_relevance: The toolbox idea (strategy depends on environment structure) can be recovered by training on LLM-generated tasks; the ecological claim holds when the environment is known.

source: Jagadish, Coda-Forno, Thalmann, Schulz & Binz (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks (ICML)
finding: Same ERMI idea on category learning: LLM-generated tasks as the ecological environment fit human category learning better than several cognitive models.
numbers: Fits human category learning better than established cognitive models across the paper's experiments (log-likelihoods not extracted).
limits: Not a heuristics test; supporting design for ecological rationality via LLMs. I read the abstract and intro only.
agent_relevance: Method to build task statistics for a given problem class cheaply.

source: Alaswad et al. (2026) Evaluating LLM-generated rules for heart disease prediction
finding: When GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.6 write simple IF-THEN rules (a frugal decision list), they predict worse than trained learners on UCI heart disease.
numbers: Random Forest 90.2% accuracy (F1 0.906); Naive Bayes 88.5%; KNN, logistic regression, decision tree 86.9% each; Claude Sonnet 4.6 rules 80.3% (F1 0.833); GPT-4o rules 70.5% (F1 0.690, recall 0.606). Rules were written without the held-out data.
limits: Single small dataset; interpretability not measured. LLM rules are not cue-validity-ordered trees in the Martignon sense.
agent_relevance: LLMs can write frugal rules, but cue order learned from data is better; do not let the agent hand-write cue orders without data.

source: Mesabah et al. (2026) MYOPIA: limits of tree-based reasoning in vision-language models
finding: A greedy, no-backtrack decision tree is a close cousin of a fast-and-frugal tree. Walking such a tree with a VLM lost to plain zero-shot in every case.
numbers: 12 of 12 dataset-model pairs (GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, MSCOCO; GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision) tree traversal below zero-shot. In one deep-tree case tree accuracy fell from 33.19% to 6.33%. Models recall labels better than they ground them in images by about 12.6 points for one model.
limits: Trees were LLM-generated, vision tasks; errors compound along the path without backtracking.
agent_relevance: Frugal sequential gates fail when each step's cue is unreliable; the cue-validity assumption must hold. Add a backtrack rule.

source: Ansari (2026) 3, 7, 14, 17, 42: instruction tuning installs and sharpens number-choice heuristics in language models
finding: Direct measurement of human-like heuristics in LLMs without sampling noise: tuning makes the number distribution less uniform in all 15 base/tuned pairs.
numbers: 18 open-weight model lines, 5 ranges up to N=100, 29 decoding configs. Tuned models almost never return endpoints; base returns endpoints at 0.30 to 0.60 of the interior rate. Round-number avoidance installed by tuning; above N=10 no modal integer is shared by more than 42% of tuned conditions.
limits: Number choice is far from judgment under uncertainty; only the idea of tuning-installed heuristics carries over.
agent_relevance: Heuristic behaviour in LLMs is partly trained in, not innate: S0 behaviour may shift between model versions.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) From prompts to trees: LLM-guided tree generation for few-shot tabular classification
finding: LLMs generate rules from world knowledge and these are organised into a decision tree for few-shot tabular classification, for fast, transparent inference.
numbers: Three-stage pipeline; reports higher accuracy and lower prompting overhead than baselines (numbers not extracted).
limits: Preprint; I read only the abstract and intro.
agent_relevance: A pattern for building a small decision-tree gate from LLM knowledge with few labelled examples.

source: Search log (2026-11-01): arXiv full-text search for LLM tests of the recognition heuristic, take-the-best, fast-and-frugal trees
finding: Negative result. Searches for recognition heuristic, fast-and-frugal with LLM, and take the best with language models returned no study that runs the founding paradigms (city size, cue-ordered paired comparison, FFT construction) on LLMs. The only LLM paper tied to take-the-best is Bogdan 2026. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited and WebSearch quota ran out, so coverage outside arXiv is incomplete.
numbers: About 14 arXiv queries; hits for ecological rationality and fast and frugal trees were all non-LLM or tangential.
limits: Absence on arXiv does not mean absence in journals (Judgment and Decision Making, Cognition).
agent_relevance: The agent cannot lean on LLM-specific evidence for the recognition heuristic; any use must be validated on our own tasks.
